results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

Every draft unit's outline summary matches the controlling idea of the spec paragraph it is aligned to, in the spec's order (p01-p04, who p05-p08, argument p09-p12, failure-patterns p40-p41, stages p16-p18, kestrel-and-pine p34-p37, organization p14/p19/p15/p20/p21/p22, decision p23/p24/p38, leaves-to-others p39, evidence p25-p30, draws-on p31-p33, living-journal p42-p44, conclusion p45-p46). The two opening callouts carry the thesis and roadmap placement and match no paragraph.
The reverse outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas.

Every unit serves its section's supporting claim: who -> S1; argument and failure patterns -> S2; stages and Kestrel & Pine -> S3; organization, decision and leaves-to-others -> S4; evidence, draws-on and living journal -> S5; the conclusion restates the claim and the two ways of reading.

Each evidence item is tied to its point: Figure 1 and Figure 2 have captions stating what they show; the three-questions, stage, parts, routing, kinds-of-statement and tiers tables are each introduced and followed by the reading rule (p17, p24, p26, the tier lead-in); the Zalando, bol, Shopify and Omnibus facts each carry the lesson they show; the incident costs in p35 are tied to facts held in four places.

results.quote: A commerce platform is usually described as a product you subscribe to, license or assemble. This book uses the word differently:
results.finding: The spec declares an elaboration that carries over Eva's five promises and the Black Friday handoffs from the opening and introduces the definition that makes those two stories one argument. At the boundary (after the voice paragraph of 'Who This Book Is For') the section opens on the usual meaning of the word with no reference back to Eva's order or Black Friday; only the word 'promises' links it, so the declared carry-over is not expressed.

results.quote: Three neighboring subjects appear only where they touch commerce architecture, and each has a book of its own on this site:
results.finding: The spec declares a contrast with the decisions the routing table sends to a chapter of this book. All other transition_in entries are expressed at their boundaries (e.g. p03 'On Black Friday 2026, the same shop', p11 'That is why', p16 'are the same for every merchant; the right answers are not', p23 'The parts are a learning path for a first reading. If a decision...', p30 'The kinds label single sentences; the tiers label the conclusions'); the closing unit links the hand-off target where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong.

results.draft_locus: Four Scale Stages, and Why Every Chapter Compares Them (stage table) and Kestrel & Pine ¶1
results.finding: Both flow readers could not tell whether 'now' is 2026 or 2027: the opening dates Eva's order 13 April 2027, Black Friday 2026 and the €48 million revenue are in 2026, and the stage table says '2023 to now'; the story's 2027 setting is explained only in 'A Living Journal' ('The story at Kestrel & Pine is set in 2027, a year after the cut-off'). The section order is fine; the prose should fix 'now' (e.g. the table cell) and say where the merchant is introduced that the story runs in 2027.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.1 (flow reader A, item 3.4)

results.quote: Every chapter in the main body of the book has a section titled
results.finding: Both flow readers could not tell what 'the main body of the book' means: it is used before the parts are laid out and is only later narrowed by 'Every chapter in Parts II to VIII answers the same five questions', leaving it unclear whether it is Parts II-VIII or I-XI. The draft can define the phrase at the point of use without citing parts by number.

results.quote: In a third, the Double Refund, 212 returns were refunded twice
results.finding: Both flow readers had to count back to make sense of 'In a third': the first incident is not numbered and the second is introduced as 'Another Kestrel & Pine order', so the ordinal does not attach to anything. A wording fix.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.8 (flow reader A, item 3.1)

results.quote: integrations get owners, contracts and reconciliation, a comparison of copies, and the company
results.finding: Both flow readers tripped on the Waypoint list: the gloss 'a comparison of copies' sits inside a comma-separated list, so the reader re-reads to see where the items end, and reconciliation (an idea already used unnamed in the three-questions table) is glossed late. The gloss should not break the list.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.6 (flow reader A, item 3.6)

results.quote: A Spaghetti Junction of unowned connectors breeds Messages in a Bottle, messages sent once and trusted, which breed Phantom Stock and Boomerangs, returns refunded twice.
results.finding: Reader A found the chain paragraph the hardest part of the page: the previous unit gives 'only their names', and this unit reasons with names whose meaning must be inferred (Spaghetti Junction, Phantom Stock, The First Snowfall) and maps one invented name onto another ('The Three-Status Order was a Schrödinger's Order'). Reader B stalled on the same passage about The First Snowfall ('in a chain of stock syncs that met real load for the first time on the day itself'), which does not obviously fit its family as given. Each pattern the paragraph reasons with needs a one-clause meaning that fits its family.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.2 (flow reader A, item 3.2)

results.quote: Chapters cite Waypoint's eight decisions by number, W1 to W8.
results.finding: Reader A only: the sentence lists about five changes and then names eight numbered decisions the reader has nothing to map onto.

results.quote: Parts II to V follow the order in the sequence it happens
results.finding: Reader A only: the claim does not match the table read just before it: Part III already reaches the books, which the journey puts last, and Part V is other channels joining the order record rather than a later step of Eva's order; A re-read the table.

results.draft_locus: The Failure Patterns ¶2 and Four Scale Stages ¶3
results.quote: in a chain of stock syncs that met real load for the first time on the day itself
results.finding: Reader B only: the stock syncs are introduced in two halves; the failure-patterns section says 'a chain of stock syncs' and only the stages section says they were hourly and produced 'the two-hour-old copy', so B paused over how a sync produced the stale copy.

results.quote: The story at Kestrel & Pine is set in 2027, a year after the cut-off
results.finding: Reader B only: currency is split across two sections, 'Why claims carry dates' in 'How to Read the Evidence' and the research cut-off two sections later in 'A Living Journal'; B suggested moving the living-journal section next to the dating rule. The split comes from the declared order (evidence, draws-on, living-journal).

Organizing principle agrees with the declared grouping: reader A reads 'subject -> how to use the book -> how far to trust it', reader B 'what the book argues -> how it is built -> how to use it -> how far to trust it', both matching the IN THIS SECTION roadmap. No section is unclear to either reader. Both noted, as mild, that Kestrel & Pine appears in the stage table before its own section, and both recommended keeping the current order (which the spec chose deliberately and the opening already introduces the merchant), so it is not counted as a material lost-thread point.
Terms reader: 'hosted platform' is never explained (rented, vendor-run platform), though one of Waypoint's key decisions rests on it; it first appears unexplained in the stage table.

results.quote: The choices evolve as Kestrel & Pine adds channels, locations and complexity.
results.finding: Terms reader: 'channel' (and 'marketplaces' as a sales channel) is used constantly but never defined; it is only implied later by the revenue split in Kestrel & Pine ¶1.

results.quote: a chain starts at a connector nobody owns
results.finding: Terms reader: 'connector' (marketplace connector, unowned connectors) is never said to be; the chain argument rests on it.
Terms reader: 'picking' and 'order line' ('an unpicked line') are not explained, which makes the Three-Status Order example harder for a reader who knows software but not commerce.

Every term on the journal's does_not_know list that the page uses is glossed at first use: SKU, system of record, idempotency, EDI, WMS, PIM, order management system (ATP, PSP, 3DS, punchout, bounded context and eventual consistency do not appear). Other unexplained terms the terms reader listed are guessable, sent to other books, or appear only in the parts or routing tables.

The opening starts on a concrete scene (Eva's order), states the five promises, gives one incident and then the thesis, audience and two ways of reading; no dictionary opener, throat-clearing or 'in this article' pattern.
The conclusion gives directions for both kinds of reader and a synthesis; it is not a bare restatement and opens no new topic.

p46 says the parts, routing table, stage tables and kinds of statement all ask which system makes a promise, which keeps it and how far the answer holds for a business of the reader's shape, and that this comes before which product to buy, matching the spec's synthesis and so_what.
The conclusion returns to Eva's five promises as five words ('this jacket, at this price, in stock, on Thursday, returnable') and makes them the index to every chapter, as the spec's callback asks.

The opening-only reader predicted, in order: who the book is for; the argument; the failure patterns; the four scale stages; the fictional merchant Kestrel & Pine; how the eleven parts follow one order; finding the chapter for a decision; what the book leaves to others; how to read the evidence and how current it is; and evidence from a worked fictional order and the 1,340-unit Black Friday incident. This matches the expected answer.

The reader stated the argument (the whole set of systems that make and keep promises; failures are a promise one system made and another could not keep; three questions) and listed the parts in order: commerce basics, catalog/price/stock, checkout to books, fulfillment, channels, integration, platform, trust, journeys, evolution, cases, as expected.
The reader opened inventory-and-availability first, because the fix is deciding which system owns stock, not making copies faster, and named systems of record and reconciliation next, as expected.
The reader labelled (a) an illustration, not an industry benchmark; (b) a recommendation with reasons and conditions; (c) an assumption not to be used as a benchmark, as expected.
The reader defined SKU as a code for a sellable variant, system of record as the authoritative home of a fact, and idempotency as a repeated request having the same effect as one, as expected.
The reader named Omnichannel because the shape decides the stage and the revenue bands are illustrative markers, not thresholds, as expected.

The reader answered no on both counts: the domain models are research maps inferred from public product behavior, real companies appear only as dated sourced cases, and the book recommends architectures, not products, as expected.
